'''Robert Martin Glaeser''' (born July 20, 1937) is an American [[biochemist]]. He is a professor emeritus of Biochemistry, Biophysics and Structural Biology at the [[University of California, Berkeley]] and a faculty scientist at [[Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory]], in [[Berkeley, California]], US. His main research area is electron diffraction and membrane models.

Glaeser is known<ref>[https://recognition.lbl.gov/lifetime-achievement-awardee-robert-martin-glaeser/ Lifetime Achievement Awardee – Robert Martin Glaeser] – Berkeley Lab</ref> for his pioneering work in [[cryogenic electron microscopy]] (cryo-EM), where he established how radiation damage was a limiting factor for imaging resolution<ref>{{cite journal|doi=10.1016/S0022-5320(71)80118-1|title=Limitations to Significant Information in Biological Electron Microscopy as a Result of Radiation Damage|year=1971|last1=Glaeser|first1=Robert M.|journal=Journal of Ultrastructure Research|volume=36|issue=3–4|pages=466–482|pmid=5107051}}</ref> and how freezing hydrated specimens allowed for more tolerance to radiation damage.<ref>{{cite journal|doi=10.1111/j.1365-2818.1978.tb01160.x|title=Radiation-Damage Relative to Transmission Electron-Microscopy of Biological Specimens at Low-Temperature|year=1978|last1=Glaeser|first1=Robert M.|last2=Taylor|first2=Kenneth A.|journal=Journal of Microscopy|volume=112|issue=1|pages=127–138|pmid=347079|s2cid=45670974}}</ref> He also pushed electron imaging microscopy resolution and contrast by studying the effect of beam-induced movement on the resolution<ref>{{cite journal|doi=10.1016/0304-3991(85)90069-5|title=Quantitative analysis of image contrast in electron micrographs of beam-sensitive crystals|year=1985|last1=Henderson|first1=Richard|last2=Glaeser|first2=Robert M.|journal=Ultramicroscopy|volume=16|issue=2|pages=139–150}}</ref> and developed methods for weak-phase imaging.<ref>{{cite journal|doi=10.1063/1.4830355|title=Methods for imaging weak-phase objects in electron microscopy|year=2013|pmid=24289381|last1=Glaeser|first1=R. M.|journal=The Review of Scientific Instruments|volume=84|issue=11|page=111101|pmc=3855062}}</ref>

Glaeser studied at the [[University of Wisconsin – Madison]] (B.A. 1959) and the [[University of California, Berkeley]] (Ph.D. 1964). He was then a postdoc at the University of Oxford (1963/64) and University of Chicago (1964/65). In 1988/89 he was a visiting scientist at the [[Max Planck Institute for Biochemistry]] (MPIB) in Martinsried near Munich, and later a professor at the [[University of California, Berkeley]].

== Awards ==
* 1983: Guggenheim Fellowship of the John Simon Guggenheim Memorial Foundation.
* 1986, President of the [[Electron Microscope Society of America]].<ref>{{cite web|url=https://microscopy.org/past-presidents|title=MSA Past Presidents|publisher= Microscopy Society of America|accessdate= 15 April 2025}}</ref>
* 2016: member of the [[American Academy of Arts and Sciences|American Academy of Arts]] and Sciences and the [[National Academy of Sciences]]<ref>[https://www.nasonline.org/directory-entry/robert-m-glaeser-cvaywd/ Robert Glaeser] – National Academy of Science</ref>
* 2018: Glenn T. Seaborg Medal<ref>[https://www.seaborg.ucla.edu/seaborg2018.html 2018 medalists] – Glenn T. Seaborg Medal</ref>
* 2021: Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory Lifetime Achievement award<ref>[https://recognition.lbl.gov/2021-laureates/ Berkeley Lab Director’s Awards for Lifetime Achievement]</ref>
